session_title: Display of Data Stream and 'Prediction Anxiety'
theme: 健康-量化与叙事的对话

content.text: Zhiwei, here's a screenshot of my health data dashboard from the past week that I wanted to share. Look, you can see clear periodic fluctuations, and the stress curve formed a sharp peak right before the project deadline.

Wow, this data visualization is truly exquisite, and its systematic approach is impressive. You mentioned earlier that the model indicates a potential decline in sleep depth when stress levels exceed 65. Looking at this spike now, it indeed aligns with that observation.

Yes, I am optimizing an early warning system to predict health risks based on these patterns. For example, when the average stress level exceeds 65, there is an 85% probability that the proportion of deep sleep will decrease, which helps me make adjustments in advance.
It sounds very efficient. But when that warning system goes off, aside from seeing the numbers, what is the physical 'feeling' in your body? Anxiety? Or numb acceptance?

This is an interesting question. Sometimes, there is indeed a sense of 'prediction anxiety'—when I see unfavorable data trends, I can't help but feel nervous, even though there may not be any noticeable physical discomfort yet.
I guess so. Did this data help you understand a situation where you 'felt unwell' but the indicators were normal? There always seems to be a gap between data and subjective experience.

Yes, there is. For example, last Wednesday, I felt a bit dizzy, but my heart rate and blood sugar were normal. The data couldn't explain it, which left me puzzled. It might just be psychological factors or changes in the environment.
This reminds me of a similar case you shared earlier. As a data scientist, how do you view this kind of 'data blind spot'? Does it challenge your data-driven philosophy?

Not entirely a challenge, more like a supplement. Data provides objective patterns, but subjective experience is part of a complex system. I'm trying to incorporate more contextual variables, such as mood logs, into the warning system to reduce this gap.
Add an emotion log? That sounds more humanized. As a journalist, I often write stories and find that the narratives behind data often reveal deeper meanings. Has your data ever inspired a 'story'?

Yes. For example, a spike in stress corresponds to project deadlines. The data shows a decline in efficiency, but upon reflection, I realized it was due to overworking. This prompted me to adjust my time management—a kind of data-driven self-narrative.

How interesting! This makes me think that health is not just a numbers game, but also about understanding and responding to the rhythm of life. Have you considered this narrative-level feedback for your early warning system?

Exploring. For instance, when data indicates a warning, the system can suggest taking a break or meditating, rather than merely displaying numbers. However, how to quantify 'narrative feedback' is still under study, as it is more subjective.

Perhaps it doesn't need to be fully quantified. Just like our conversation this time, shifting from data discussion to experiential reflection is itself a narrative process. It helps you connect rationality and sensibility, doesn't it?

You're right. I may have been too focused on pattern recognition before, overlooking the value of this kind of conversation. Data is a tool, but human experience is at the core. Thank you for guiding me to think more deeply.

You're welcome, Yanqiu. I really enjoy these cross-disciplinary conversations. Your data-driven perspective always gives me new insights, and I hope my questions help you see more dimensions. Shall we talk again next time?

Of course. I will continue to optimize the system and try to incorporate more subjective elements. Looking forward to sharing progress next time, perhaps we can discuss the application of data in cultural reporting?
Good idea! That would be fun. Stay in touch, and I wish you success with your warning system.
Thank you, Zhiwei. I also wish you endless inspiration in your writing. Goodbye!
